structures.name: sternocleidomastoid
structures.definition: Strap-like neck muscle running from the sternum and clavicle up to the mastoid process.
structures.function: Turns the head to the opposite side and tilts it to the same side; both together flex the neck.
structures.why: It positions the head and lifts the sternum as an accessory breathing muscle when breathing is hard.

notes.nursing: Visible use of the neck muscles when breathing at rest is a sign of respiratory distress.
notes.medicine: Shortening in infancy causes torticollis; it divides the neck into anterior and posterior triangles.
notes.physio: Often tight in forward-head posture; stretched in neck rehabilitation.

structures.name: levator scapulae
structures.definition: Muscle running from the upper cervical vertebrae down to the upper inner corner of the shoulder blade.
structures.function: Elevates the scapula and tips the glenoid downward; helps bend the neck to the side.
structures.why: It works with the upper back muscles to lift and steady the shoulder blade.

notes.physio: A common source of the stiff, painful neck sometimes called a crick in the neck.

structures.name: scalene muscles
structures.definition: Three muscles on each side of the neck running from the cervical vertebrae to the first two ribs.
structures.function: Raise the first two ribs in deep breathing and bend the neck to the side.
structures.why: They anchor the top of the rib cage so the chest can expand upward.

notes.medicine: The brachial plexus and subclavian artery pass between the anterior and middle muscles: the site of interscalene nerve blocks and thoracic outlet compression.
notes.nursing: Their use during breathing at rest is a sign of respiratory distress.

structures.name: digastric
structures.definition: Two-bellied muscle under the jaw, its bellies joined by a tendon slung near the hyoid bone.
structures.function: Opens the mouth by pulling the mandible down and raises the hyoid during swallowing.
structures.why: Two bellies on one tendon let a single muscle pull the jaw and the hyoid from two directions.

notes.dentistry: Helps open the mouth; its anterior belly is supplied by the trigeminal nerve and its posterior belly by the facial nerve.

structures.name: mylohyoid
structures.definition: Thin sheet of muscle forming the floor of the mouth between the two halves of the mandible.
structures.function: Raises the floor of the mouth and the hyoid bone during swallowing and speech.
structures.why: It forms a muscular sling that supports the tongue.

notes.dentistry: Lower molar roots lie below its attachment line, so infections there spread into the neck rather than under the tongue.

structures.name: deltoid
structures.definition: Thick triangular muscle that caps the shoulder.
structures.function: Raises the arm away from the body; its front part flexes and its back part extends the arm.
structures.why: Wrapping over the shoulder joint, it gives the arm power to lift in almost any direction.

notes.nursing: Deltoid IM injection: 2–3 fingerbreadths below the acromion into the thickest part; up to about 1 mL in adults.
notes.medicine: Supplied by the axillary nerve, which is at risk in shoulder dislocation and surgical neck fractures.
notes.sports: Overhead presses and lateral raises train its three parts.

structures.name: pectoralis major
structures.definition: Large fan-shaped chest muscle running from the sternum and clavicle to the upper humerus.
structures.function: Pulls the arm across the chest, rotates it inward and helps flex the shoulder.
structures.why: Its broad fan gives power for pushing, climbing and hugging.

notes.sports: Trained by bench press and push-ups; its humeral tendon can rupture during heavy bench pressing.
notes.medicine: Forms the anterior axillary fold.

structures.name: pectoralis minor
structures.definition: Small triangular muscle under the large chest muscle, attached to the coracoid process.
structures.function: Pulls the scapula forward and down and lifts the ribs in forced breathing.
structures.why: It steadies the shoulder blade against the chest wall.

notes.physio: Tightness tilts the scapula forward and is linked to rounded shoulders and impingement.

structures.name: serratus anterior
structures.definition: Saw-toothed muscle on the side of the chest, from the upper ribs to the inner edge of the shoulder blade.
structures.function: Pulls the scapula forward around the ribs and rotates it upward so the arm can go overhead.
structures.why: It holds the shoulder blade flat against the chest wall.

notes.medicine: Long thoracic nerve injury, for example during axillary surgery, causes winging of the scapula.
notes.physio: Strengthened with push-up plus and wall slides in scapular rehabilitation.
notes.sports: Called the boxer’s muscle because it drives a punch forward.

structures.name: rotator cuff
structures.definition: Four muscles whose tendons wrap the head of the humerus to hold it in its shallow socket.
structures.function: Keep the humeral head centred in the glenoid and rotate the arm.
structures.why: The shoulder trades bony stability for range of motion, so these muscles hold it together.

notes.physio: Cuff tendinopathy and tears are among the commonest shoulder problems; progressive loading is first-line treatment.
notes.sports: Throwers and swimmers need cuff endurance; weakness at the back of the cuff is linked to injury.
notes.medicine: Remember SITS: supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis.

structures.name: supraspinatus
structures.definition: Muscle lying in the fossa above the spine of the scapula, its tendon running under the acromion.
structures.function: Starts raising the arm sideways and presses the humeral head into its socket.
structures.why: Its pull holds the ball in the socket while the larger shoulder muscle lifts.

notes.physio: Its tendon is the one most often involved in impingement and cuff tears (painful arc between about 60° and 120°).

structures.name: infraspinatus
structures.definition: Muscle filling the fossa below the spine of the scapula.
structures.function: Rotates the arm outward and steadies the shoulder.
structures.why: It balances the strong inward rotators so the shoulder stays centred.

notes.sports: Tightness and weakness at the back of the shoulder are common in throwing athletes.

structures.name: teres minor
structures.definition: Small cylindrical muscle along the outer border of the shoulder blade.
structures.function: Rotates the arm outward and helps hold the humeral head in place.
structures.why: A second outward rotator that backs up its larger neighbour above.

notes.medicine: Supplied by the axillary nerve, like the deltoid.

structures.name: subscapularis
structures.definition: Large muscle on the rib-facing surface of the shoulder blade.
structures.function: Rotates the arm inward and protects the front of the shoulder joint.
structures.why: The only cuff muscle at the front, it guards against the shoulder dislocating forward.

notes.physio: Tested with the lift-off and belly-press tests.

structures.name: teres major
structures.definition: Thick muscle running from the lower angle of the scapula to the front of the humerus.
structures.function: Pulls the arm down and back and rotates it inward.
structures.why: It assists the large back muscle (latissimus dorsi) in powerful pulling.

notes.medicine: Forms the lower border of the quadrangular and triangular spaces at the back of the shoulder.

structures.name: rhomboids
structures.definition: Two flat muscles running from the spine to the inner border of the shoulder blade.
structures.function: Pull the shoulder blades together and up.
structures.why: They keep the shoulder blades from drifting forward and away from the spine.

notes.physio: Weakness contributes to rounded shoulders; trained with rows and scapular retraction.

structures.name: biceps brachii
structures.definition: Two-headed muscle on the front of the upper arm.
structures.function: Bends the elbow and turns the palm upward; helps flex the shoulder.
structures.why: Crossing both shoulder and elbow, it is strongest when lifting with the palm up or turning a screwdriver.

notes.nursing: Its tendon is felt in the antecubital fossa; the brachial pulse, used for blood pressure, lies just medial to it.
notes.medicine: The biceps reflex tests C5–C6; rupture of the long head gives a “Popeye” bulge.
notes.sports: Its distal tendon can rupture under a sudden heavy lowering load.

structures.name: triceps brachii
structures.definition: Three-headed muscle on the back of the upper arm.
structures.function: Straightens the elbow; its long head also extends the shoulder.
structures.why: The main elbow extensor, used in pushing and getting up from a chair.

notes.nursing: Skinfold thickness for nutritional assessment is measured over the back of the arm at its midpoint.
notes.medicine: The triceps reflex tests C7.

structures.name: brachialis
structures.definition: Muscle deep to the front upper-arm muscle, attached to the coronoid process of the ulna.
structures.function: The main flexor of the elbow in every forearm position.
structures.why: Attached to the ulna, which does not rotate, it flexes the elbow whatever the palm is doing.

notes.medicine: Can calcify after elbow injury (myositis ossificans), so avoid aggressive massage after trauma.

structures.name: brachioradialis
structures.definition: Forearm muscle running from the lower outer humerus to the radius near the wrist.
structures.function: Bends the elbow, most strongly with the forearm half-turned, as when holding a mug.
structures.why: A long lever across the elbow that adds speed and power to bending it.

notes.medicine: The brachioradialis reflex tests C6.

structures.name: pronator teres
structures.definition: Short forearm muscle running from the medial epicondyle across to the middle of the radius.
structures.function: Turns the palm down and helps bend the elbow.
structures.why: It rolls the radius over the ulna so the hand can face downward.

notes.medicine: The median nerve passes between its two heads and can be compressed there (pronator syndrome).

structures.name: flexor carpi radialis
structures.definition: Forearm muscle running from the medial epicondyle to the base of the second metacarpal.
structures.function: Bends the wrist and tilts it toward the thumb side.
structures.why: Part of the forearm flexor group that powers gripping.

notes.nursing: Its tendon is a landmark at the wrist: the radial pulse is felt just lateral to it.

structures.name: flexor digitorum superficialis
structures.definition: Forearm muscle whose four tendons attach to the middle bones of the fingers.
structures.function: Bends the fingers at their middle joints and helps bend the wrist.
structures.why: It lets each finger flex on its own for grip and fine tasks.

notes.medicine: Tested by holding the other fingers straight and asking for one finger to bend at its middle joint.

structures.name: extensor digitorum
structures.definition: Muscle on the back of the forearm whose tendons spread over the backs of the fingers.
structures.function: Straightens the fingers and helps extend the wrist.
structures.why: It opens the hand to let go, balancing the strong finger flexors.

notes.physio: Overload at its origin on the lateral epicondyle contributes to tennis elbow.

structures.name: trapezius
structures.definition: Large diamond-shaped muscle covering the back of the neck and upper back.
structures.function: Lifts, pulls back and lowers the shoulder blade and rotates it upward when the arm goes overhead.
structures.why: Its three parts let the shoulder blade move in many directions and hold the shoulder up against the arm’s weight.

notes.medicine: Supplied by the accessory nerve (CN XI); injury causes a drooping shoulder and weak shrug.
notes.physio: Upper fibres are often overactive and lower fibres weak in shoulder impingement.
notes.sports: Shrugs train the upper part; rows and prone Y-raises train the middle and lower parts.

structures.name: diaphragm
structures.definition: Dome-shaped sheet of muscle separating the chest from the abdomen.
structures.function: The main muscle of breathing: it flattens as it contracts, drawing air into the lungs.
structures.why: By enlarging the chest from below, it does most of the work of quiet breathing.

notes.nursing: Sitting a breathless patient upright lets it move more freely.
notes.medicine: Supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3–C5); irritation refers pain to the shoulder tip.
notes.physio: Diaphragmatic breathing exercises improve breathing efficiency after surgery.

structures.name: external oblique
structures.definition: The largest and most superficial flat muscle of the side of the abdomen; its fibres run down and forward like hands in front pockets.
structures.function: Flexes and rotates the trunk and compresses the abdomen.
structures.why: With the other abdominal muscles it forms a corset that protects the organs and supports the spine.

notes.medicine: Its aponeurosis forms the inguinal ligament and the front wall of the inguinal canal.
notes.sports: Trained with rotation and anti-rotation core exercises.

structures.name: erector spinae
structures.definition: Column of muscles running alongside the spine from the pelvis to the skull.
structures.function: Straightens the back, controls bending forward and bends the spine to the side.
structures.why: It holds the body upright against gravity all day.

notes.physio: Back extensor endurance is a treatment target in low back pain.
notes.sports: Trained by deadlifts and back extensions; it often guards painfully after a back strain.

structures.name: external intercostals
structures.definition: Muscles filling the spaces between the ribs, their fibres running down and forward.
structures.function: Lift the ribs when breathing in.
structures.why: They stiffen and raise the chest wall so it doesn’t get sucked inward on each breath.

notes.medicine: The neurovascular bundle runs in the groove under each rib, between the deeper layers.

structures.name: gluteus maximus
structures.definition: Large, thick muscle forming most of the buttock.
structures.function: Extends and turns the hip outward, as in climbing stairs, running and rising from a chair.
structures.why: Its size reflects upright walking: it stops the trunk tipping forward at the hip.

notes.nursing: The dorsogluteal injection site risks the sciatic nerve; the ventrogluteal site is preferred.
notes.physio: Weakness is linked to knee and back pain; bridges and squats retrain it.
notes.sports: A main driver of sprint acceleration and jumping.

structures.name: gluteus medius
structures.definition: Fan-shaped hip muscle on the outer surface of the ilium, partly covered by the largest buttock muscle.
structures.function: Abducts the hip and keeps the pelvis level when standing on one leg.
structures.why: Every step balances on one leg; without it the pelvis drops on the other side.

notes.nursing: The ventrogluteal IM injection site lies in this muscle, away from major nerves and vessels.
notes.physio: Weakness causes a Trendelenburg gait.

structures.name: gluteus minimus
structures.definition: The smallest and deepest of the three buttock muscles.
structures.function: Abducts and turns the hip inward and steadies the pelvis.
structures.why: It works with its larger neighbour to keep the pelvis level while walking.

notes.physio: Its tendon is often involved in lateral hip pain (gluteal tendinopathy).

structures.name: piriformis
structures.definition: Pear-shaped muscle running from the front of the sacrum to the greater trochanter.
structures.function: Rotates the hip outward and moves the bent hip out to the side.
structures.why: One of the deep hip rotators that steady the femoral head in its socket.

notes.medicine: The sciatic nerve usually leaves the pelvis just below it; compression here is called piriformis syndrome.

structures.name: tensor fasciae latae
structures.definition: Small muscle on the outer front of the hip that blends into the iliotibial tract.
structures.function: Helps flex, abduct and turn the hip inward and steadies the knee through the iliotibial band.
structures.why: It tightens the fascia of the thigh to stabilise hip and knee when standing on one leg.

notes.sports: Overuse with a tight iliotibial band contributes to outer knee pain in runners.

structures.name: iliopsoas
structures.definition: Combined muscle formed by the psoas major from the lumbar spine and the iliacus from the pelvis, inserting on the lesser trochanter.
structures.function: The strongest hip flexor, lifting the thigh toward the trunk.
structures.why: It links the spine to the leg, flexing the hip in walking, running and sitting up.

notes.physio: Long periods of sitting can shorten it; the Thomas test assesses its length.
notes.medicine: Inflammation next to it (psoas abscess, appendicitis) makes hip extension painful: the psoas sign.

structures.name: sartorius
structures.definition: Long strap-like muscle crossing the thigh diagonally from the anterior superior iliac spine to the inner tibia.
structures.function: Flexes, abducts and turns the hip outward and bends the knee, as when sitting cross-legged.
structures.why: The longest muscle in the body, it moves hip and knee together.

notes.medicine: Forms the lateral border of the femoral triangle.

structures.name: quadriceps femoris
structures.definition: Four-part muscle group on the front of the thigh, joined in one tendon around the kneecap.
structures.function: Straightens the knee; one part also flexes the hip.
structures.why: It controls the knee when standing up, climbing and landing.

notes.physio: Wasting starts within days of knee injury or surgery; early static contractions limit it.
notes.sports: Strength in lowering (eccentric) movements protects the knee in landing and cutting.
notes.nursing: The knee-jerk reflex tests its nerve supply (L3–L4).

structures.name: rectus femoris
structures.definition: Straight muscle down the middle of the front of the thigh, the only one of its group to cross the hip.
structures.function: Flexes the hip and straightens the knee.
structures.why: Crossing two joints lets it power a kick.

notes.nursing: An alternative IM site in adults, used less often because injections there are painful.

structures.name: vastus lateralis
structures.definition: The largest muscle of the front-of-thigh group, on the outer side of the thigh.
structures.function: Straightens the knee.
structures.why: It provides much of the force for standing and climbing.

notes.nursing: The preferred IM site in infants: the middle third of the thigh on its front-outer side.

structures.name: vastus medialis
structures.definition: Teardrop-shaped muscle on the inner side of the lower thigh, just above the knee.
structures.function: Straightens the knee and helps keep the kneecap tracking centrally.
structures.why: Its lowest fibres pull the patella inward, balancing the pull of the larger outer muscle.

notes.physio: Targeted in rehabilitation of patellofemoral pain.

structures.name: vastus intermedius
structures.definition: Deep muscle lying under the straight central thigh muscle, directly on the front of the femur.
structures.function: Straightens the knee.
structures.why: It adds force to knee extension from directly in front of the femur.

notes.medicine: A thigh bruise (“dead leg”) can bleed into it and, rarely, calcify.

structures.name: adductor longus
structures.definition: Fan-shaped inner-thigh muscle running from the pubis to the middle of the femur.
structures.function: Pulls the thigh inward and helps flex it.
structures.why: It stabilises the pelvis and brings the legs together.

notes.sports: Groin strains most often involve this muscle, typically in football and ice hockey.
notes.medicine: Forms the medial border of the femoral triangle.

structures.name: adductor magnus
structures.definition: The largest and deepest inner-thigh muscle, running from the pubis and ischial tuberosity along the femur.
structures.function: Pulls the thigh inward; its hamstring part also extends the hip.
structures.why: A powerful stabiliser of the hip in squatting and climbing.

notes.medicine: The femoral artery passes through a gap in its tendon (adductor hiatus) to become the popliteal artery.

structures.name: gracilis
structures.definition: Long, slender muscle on the inner thigh from the pubis to the inner tibia.
structures.function: Pulls the thigh inward and bends the knee.
structures.why: The most superficial of the inner-thigh group, it helps bring the legs together.

notes.medicine: Its tendon is harvested, often with semitendinosus, for ACL reconstruction.

structures.name: hamstrings
structures.definition: Three muscles on the back of the thigh running from the ischial tuberosity to just below the knee.
structures.function: Bend the knee and extend the hip.
structures.why: They slow the swinging leg when running and protect the knee.

notes.sports: The commonest muscle strain in sprinting; Nordic curls reduce the risk.
notes.physio: The straight leg raise assesses their length as well as nerve tension.

structures.name: biceps femoris
structures.definition: Two-headed muscle on the outer back of the thigh, inserting on the head of the fibula.
structures.function: Bends the knee, turns the bent knee outward, and its long head extends the hip.
structures.why: It is the outer member of the back-of-thigh group.

notes.sports: Its long head is the part most often strained in sprinters.

structures.name: semitendinosus
structures.definition: Inner back-of-thigh muscle with a long cord-like tendon in its lower half.
structures.function: Bends the knee, turns the bent knee inward and extends the hip.
structures.why: Its long tendon joins the pes anserinus on the inner tibia.

notes.medicine: Often harvested with gracilis for ACL reconstruction.

structures.name: semimembranosus
structures.definition: Broad, flat muscle of the inner back of the thigh, lying under its tendon-rich neighbour.
structures.function: Bends the knee, turns the bent knee inward and extends the hip.
structures.why: The deepest and broadest of its group, it also reinforces the back of the knee capsule.

notes.physio: A Baker’s cyst often arises between it and the medial head of the calf muscle.

structures.name: gastrocnemius
structures.definition: Two-headed muscle forming the bulge of the calf, crossing both knee and ankle.
structures.function: Points the foot and helps bend the knee.
structures.why: It gives push-off power for walking, running and jumping.

notes.nursing: Calf pain, swelling and warmth may mean deep vein thrombosis; assess and escalate.
notes.physio: Tightness limits ankle dorsiflexion; tested with the knee straight.
notes.sports: “Tennis leg” is a tear of its medial head.

structures.name: soleus
structures.definition: Broad, flat muscle lying deep to the main calf muscle.
structures.function: Points the foot and keeps the body from falling forward when standing.
structures.why: Rich in fatigue-resistant fibres, it works almost constantly while you stand.

notes.nursing: Its veins act as a muscle pump; immobility stops the pump and raises the risk of DVT.
notes.physio: Stretched with the knee bent to target it rather than the two-headed calf muscle.

structures.name: tibialis anterior
structures.definition: Muscle running down the front of the shin to the inner side of the foot.
structures.function: Lifts the foot and turns the sole inward.
structures.why: It lifts the toes clear of the ground as the leg swings through each step.

notes.medicine: Weakness, for example from common fibular nerve palsy, causes foot drop and a high-stepping gait.
notes.sports: Overuse contributes to pain at the front of the shin in runners.

structures.name: fibularis longus
structures.definition: Long muscle on the outer side of the leg whose tendon passes behind the lateral malleolus and under the foot.
structures.function: Turns the sole outward, points the foot and supports the arches.
structures.why: It stops the ankle rolling over and steadies the foot on uneven ground.

notes.sports: Retraining it after an ankle sprain improves eversion strength and balance.
